definition: An exclusive right granted by the state that forbids others from competing in some activity, such as making or selling a product.
A private agreement, usually attached to a property deed, that limits how the owners who signed it may use their land.

A right over someone else’s property that lets you forbid certain uses of it rather than use it yourself, such as stopping a neighbor from building above a certain height. Also called a negative easement.
An early modern economic policy of using state grants, monopolies and trade restrictions to enrich the crown and favored domestic producers.
Free, standardized licenses that let creators give permission in advance, for example to share a work as long as they are credited, instead of negotiating each use.
The usual justification for patents: inventors get a temporary monopoly in exchange for publicly disclosing how their invention works.
Two US bills (2011–2012) that would have let authorities and rights holders block websites accused of piracy. They were shelved in January 2012 after widespread online protests.
A trade agreement among twelve Pacific Rim countries, including the United States, whose intellectual-property chapter would have lengthened copyright terms and toughened enforcement.
Judging a policy by its estimated total costs and benefits, rather than by principles such as property rights or justice.
Libertarians influenced by the Austrian school of economics (Ludwig von Mises, Murray Rothbard and others), which reasons from principles of human action rather than statistical models.
The first British copyright law (1710). It gave authors, rather than the printers’ guild, the exclusive right to print their books for a limited term: 14 years, renewable once.
The London guild of printers and booksellers, which held a crown-granted monopoly over printing in England until the late 1600s.
Works still under copyright whose owners can’t be identified or found, so nobody can get permission to reprint or reuse them.
The practice of companies that own patents but make nothing, earning money mainly by threatening or filing infringement lawsuits.
A 1998 US copyright law. Its notice-and-takedown procedure lets anyone claiming a copyright get material removed from sites like YouTube, usually without a court looking at it first.
A patent obtained mainly to deter lawsuits: if a competitor sues, you can countersue with patents of your own.
An arrangement in which companies share patents with one another, often so that members can defend themselves against lawsuits together.
